list.listitem: The appearance, timing and duration of lesions are key to diagnosing polymorphous light eruption (PMLE). The age and gender of the patient are also helpful. C

Avoidance of sunlight is an absolute must. Patients need explicit instructions on proper use of sunscreen and sun protection. One ounce of sun screen, or the size of a shot glass, is needed to cover a person's face, arms and legs and must be reapplied every 2 hours and after water activities. C

background.definition: Polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) is the most common idiopathic photodermatosis. It is characterized by lesions that vary in appearance and are generally localized to sun-exposed skin. Symptoms of PMLE are intermittent and transient. Lesions appear minutes to hours after sun exposures in early spring and summer, during vacations to sunny or high-altitude locales, or after exposure from ultraviolet light (UVL) in tanning beds.

list.listitem: Estimated to affect 10% to 20% North America and European populations.
Prevalence estimates are lower in southern latitudes such as Australia (4.3%).
Many people who are aware they have a "sun rash" never seek medical treatment so estimations may be low.
PMLE is caused by a combination of genetics (possibly expression of a form of heat shock protein) and environment (exposure to ultraviolet radiation [UVR]).
PMLE is considered a delayed hypersensitivity (DTH) response to endogenous cutaneous photo-induced antigen(s).

One study of timed biopsies from PMLE lesions found perivascular infiltrates of mainly CD4+ T lymphocytes within a few hours of UVR exposure and CD8+ lymphocytes after a few days, a pattern that suggests DTH.
The antigen responsible for this response is unclear but one study found a form of heat-shock protein.
Both UVB and UVA radiation and rarely visible light trigger lesions in PMLE. UVR-induced expression of proinflammatory genes in human keratinocytes is thought to be important for the pathogenesis.
Increased expression of keratinocyte-derived proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-8) and adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1, and ICAM-1) have been found in lesional skin of patients with PMLE.
Other proinflammatory cytokines, IL-10 and TNF alpha, are also found in UVA-irradiated keratinocytes.
Sun avoidance, sun protection, and broad spectrum sunscreen applied properly are the mainstay in prevention of PMLE and other photosensitive dermatoses. C
Take a thorough history for prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal medications, as well as skin care products and sunscreens that may cause a photoallergy or phototoxic reaction (). C
Ask about other underlying skin conditions that may be exacerbated by the sun or UVL (). C
If sun sensitivity has been present since birth or early childhood consider a porphyria or genodermatosis ( and ). C
A skin biopsy and ANA are not necessary to diagnose polymorphous light eruption (PMLE) but are helpful to distinguish it from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). C
Lesions of PMLE appear minutes to hours after sunlight or tanning bed exposure. Attacks most often occur in early spring and summer or during vacations to sunny or high-altitude locales.

PMLE lesions vary in appearance from erythematous to skin colored papules, papulovesicles, vesicles or plaques and are pruritic. They are generally localized to sun-exposed skin with a symmetric but patchy distribution. Common areas are the cheeks, nose, chin, back, sides of the neck, upper chest, outer arms, shins, and dorsal hands/feet.
Rarely there may be systemic symptoms such as malaise, headache, fever, nausea.
Symptoms are intermittent and transient and typically last a few days but may persist for several weeks.
Episodes tend to diminish or experience "hardening" over the course of the summer and most patients are symptom free during the winter in northern climates.
Onset can be any age but typically is in the second and third decade. PMLE is found in all races, all parts of the world, and is more common in women (2:1).

PMLE can often be differentiated from the other idiopathic photodermatoses based on clinical history and physical alone. Of the other photosensitive dermatoses, systemic or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SLE/SCLE) are the most important disorders to distinguish. This can be done with a skin biopsy and lab work.

Skin biopsy: classic lesions will have fibrin stranding within massive papillary dermal edema plus a mild to moderate superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, unlike SLE or SCLE in which the lymphocytic infiltrate may be similar but should also be peri-eccrine. SLE/SCLE classically displays an interface dermatitis with interstitial mucin instead of dermal edema as in PMLE.
Photopatch testing: not routinely performed in a clinical setting but approximately 60% of patients will have positive results to UVA > UVB > UVA/UVB combined.
ANA, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies are usually negative. Direct immunofluorescence of lesional skin biopsy is also typically negative. This can help distinguish SLE/SCLE and porphyrias from PMLE.

PMLE is a photodermatosis. There are many other skin conditions that present with photosensitivity and some can be diagnosed simply on clinical findings or history. Others require lab work or other testing.

The differential diagnosis of dermatoses with photosensitivity includes idiopathic photodermatoses (), phototoxic or photoallergic reactions (), photo-aggravated dermatoses (), genodermatoses with photosensitivity (), and porphyrias ( and ).
Hardening through ultraviolet A (UVA) or psoralen + UVA (PUVA) is helpful but requires a facility that is equipped for light therapy. UVB is available for home devices. B
Topical corticosteroids will help most patients control the symptoms. C

Topical corticosteroids can help with flares in many patients. Low potency ones such as hydrocortisone or desonide are safe for the face. Mid to high potency ones such as triamcinolone or fluocinonide are safe for arms, trunk or legs.
Systemic corticosteroids are rarely needed but effective for extreme flares.
Antihistamines are not very helpful but sometimes reduce pruritus.
Antimalarials may have a small clinical benefit.
Thalidomide has been used with some success but teratogenic side effects limit its use since this is most commonly a disease of young women.
Azathioprine and cyclosporine have been successful in severe refractory cases on a short term basis.
Topical antioxidants; flavonoids, vitamins C and E may be helpful to reduce oxidative stress in the skin and prevent symptoms more than sunscreen alone.

Oral beta-carotene taken orally partially reduced sun sensitivity in 23 of 100 treatment periods with full freedom of sun sensitivity in 6 of 100. This was a double blind crossover study of 40 patients with PMLE over three summers. Patients received, either placebo, oxychloroquine, or 100 mg beta-carotene/canthaxanthin. The chloroquine treatment periods had similar success to carotenoids.

A randomised placebo controlled double blinded study in 60 patients showed reduction of PLE after 1 exposure of UVA after 12 weeks intake of lycopene, beta-carotene and lactobacillus johnsonii (p < 0.001). This effect was not present after 2 exposures of UVA.
Short course desensitisation treatment with narrow band UVB twice a week for 4 weeks with hardening sustained in 87.5%. The period of this benefit needed to be defined clearly.
Oral nicotinamide has shown mixed efficacy in small trials.

Sun avoidance, sun protective clothing, and broad spectrum sunscreens to block UVA and UVB are essential for prevention and treatment. Patients need careful instruction on appropriate coverage and appropriate amount of sunscreen.
UVB, UVA or psoralen + UVA (PUVA) can induce hardening.
Most patients with PMLE will improve slowly over many years and may even be cured later in life. B

There is no greater risk of SLE/SCLE developing in patients with PMLE but if high ANA titers are found initially or other symptoms develop, further investigation is warranted because PMLE may be the form fruste of SLE/SCLE. C
A higher incidence of thyroid disease (14%) was found in one study. B

tr.td: Papules and vesicles on light-exposed areas of the ears usually in the early springtime. Primarily affects boys and young men.
Pruritic crusted papules on face and limbs with cheilitis. Can occur on covered skin. Occurs in children, especially Native Americans. Improves by adolescence. Heals with scarring.
Onset in childhood of pruritic or blistering lesions on face. Often blister and form hemorrhagic crusts. Heals with scarring.
Occurs mostly in older men. Believed to be delayed type hypersensitivity response to unknown photoallergen. Persistent eczematous eruption on face, neck, upper chest, and dorsal arms.
Wheals (hives) appear within minutes of ultraviolet radiation exposure on skin. Lesions last less than 24 hours.

feature.caption: Genodermatoses with Photosensitivity.
feature.feature_body:
Genodermatoses with Photosensitivity Inheritance Clinical Features
Xeroderma pigmentosa XR Lentigines (sun spots), early onset photosensitivity, skin cancers, photophobia, neurologic abnormalities
Bloom's syndrome AR Malar erythema and telangiectasia, short stature, recurrent infections, increase frequency of lymphoma/leukemia
Cockayne's syndrome AR Cachexia, large low set ears, short stature, progressive deafness
Rothmund-Thompson syndrome AR Poikiloderma, short stature, spares hair, juvenile cataracts, skeletal dysplasia, skin cancer, osteogenic sarcoma
Trichothiodystrophy AR Brittle hair, microcephaly, receding chin, protruding ears, erythroderma, nail dystrophy, mental and growth retardation
Kindler syndrome Sporadic/AR Acral bullae (hands/feet), poikiloderma, atrophy
Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) AD Odontogenic cysts, calcified flax cerebri, macrocephaly, palmar pits, multiple basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma
XR, X-linked recessive; AR, autosomal recessive; AD, autosomal dominant. Adapted from Bolognia J, Jorizzo J, Rapini R, eds. Dermatology. New York: Mosby. 2004.

feature.caption: Porphyrias with Photosensitivity.
feature.feature_body:
Porphyrias with Photosensitivity Dermatologic Features Positive Porphyrin Specimens Inheritance
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) Most common porphyria, skin fragility, blisters, erosions, crusts, milia and scarring on dorsal hands, face, bald scalp; hypertrichosis; hyperpigmentation; sclerodermoid changes plasma, urine and stool urine fluoresces pink with Wood's lamp (black light) AD (<25%) acquired
Erythropoietic protoporphyria Onset early childhood; Child screams in pain when going outside; erythema, edema, purpura, erosions, usually no blisters; waxy scars on nose and dorsal hands, 5% may have severe liver disease plasma, stool AD
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria Onset infancy/early childhood; very severe, mutilating photosensitivity; hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, red teeth, loss of eyelashes, necrotizing scleritis, hemolytic anemia, hepatosplenomegaly plasma, urine, stool urine may fluoresce AR
Hereditary coproporphyria onset after puberty, erythema and blistering, acute attacks like acute intermittent porphyria (neurocutaneous porphyria) plasma, urine, stool urine fluoresces AD
Hepatoerythrocytic porphyria (familial PCT) Onset infancy, variant of PCT with marked to severe phototoxicity and scarring plasma, urine, stool urine fluoresces AR
Variegate porphyria Onset 2nd to 3rd decade, similar to PCT + acute attacks (neurocutaneous porphyria), more common in South Africa plasma, urine, stool plasma fluoresces at 625 nm, urine may fluoresce AD
Pseudoporphyria Similar to PCT NONE See for causes
AR, autosomal recessive; AD, autosomal dominant. Adapted from Bolognia J, Jorizzo J, Rapini R, eds. Dermatology. New York: Mosby. 2004.
